title: Many species need a large local stock to persist

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Many species need a large local stock to persist

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: In many cases a large number of individuals of a species, relative to the number of its enemies, is necessary for the species to survive, which explains why rare plants can be very abundant in the few spots where they occur.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: On the other hand, in many cases, a large stock of individuals of the same species, relatively to the numbers of its enemies, is absolutely necessary for its preservation.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter III, “Struggle for Existence”; section “Protection from the number of individuals”. Scope: plants and animals subject to predation, e.g. seed crops eaten by birds

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch03-08: needs-new-data, resolvability 0.51

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The mechanism has a clear density-dependent test, but current global datasets provide only coarse proxies. Adequate replicated population-enemy time series would need to be collected or compiled from new observations.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Estimate persistence probability against conspecific density and enemy density across populations, looking for a positive threshold or Allee effect; then test whether range-restricted plants have high abundance within occupied sites. A widespread enemy-relative threshold supports the mechanism.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Enemy and absolute density time series are rarely paired.

Opportunistic occurrences cannot identify persistence thresholds.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Plot databases can test the biogeographic pattern that some rare plants are locally numerous, and a few demographic models speak to Allee effects. Enemy-relative stock size, which is the mechanism, is usually missing. The result can support or weaken the pattern for plants and only proxy the survival rule.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Test for positive density dependence at low density in demographic models, and test whether geographically rare plants are locally abundant where they occur, relative to their enemies' density. Allee effects plus locally high density of range-restricted plants would support the statement; strictly negative density dependence and rare plants that are also locally sparse would count against it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Most matrix models are not density-dependent, so Allee effects are a small, biased subset.

Enemy density is rarely recorded in the same plots as the plant census.

Local abundance of rare plants can reflect habitat specialization rather than swamping of enemies.
